Posttraumatic Shoulder Stiffness
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Background
Secondary causes of shoulder stiffness include those with a known cause, including
posttraumatic or surgical stiffness. Posttraumatic shoulder stiffness is linked to a soft-tissue
injury or fracture and usually is associated with a period of immobilization.1,2
Overview
Posttraumatic stiffness is a nuanced condition.
No clear definition of stiffness is agreed on.
Stiffness is defined as limitation of active and passive motion, which are approximately equal
in limitation.
Dissimilar from primary shoulder stiffness or frozen shoulder, in which the pathoanatomy has
been studied, posttraumatic stiffness is not as well understood.

Overview
Posttraumatic shoulder stiffness is multifaceted. Causal mechanisms of posttraumatic
shoulder stiffness are vast and include extra-articular adhesions tethering the motion of
the shoulder; hematomas; burn injuries; neurologic deficits, including cervical spine and
brachial plexopathies; periarticular fractures; intra-articular loose bodies; acute tendon
ruptures; and scarring of the capsule secondary to adjacent trauma.
Although no clear definition of posttraumatic shoulder stiffness exists, some research
has used forward flexion/elevation of less than 100° and external rotation of less than
50% of that of the contralateral side or that of age-matched controls as cutoff values for
inclusion in their studies;3 these cutoff values were reported previously in primary
adhesive capsulitis.4
Classification

2/28

Posttraumatic shoulder stiffness: has a known cause, not related to surgery
Extra-articular/neurologic: adhesions outside the joint impairing the motion interface by
mechanically blocking, tethering, or impairing with neurophysiologic deficits (eg, heterotopic
ossification, skin scarring from burns, muscle tightness, injuries to the cervical spine or
brachial plexus)
Capsular: fibrosis of the capsule after defined trauma
Intra-articular: injuries to the intra-articular structures (eg, fractures, chondral lesions, labral
tear, loose bodies, tendon tear)
Anatomic grouping of posttraumatic stiffness is a result of damage to the shoulder joint and
can be divided into three groups: extra-articular, capsular, or intra-articular.1 These can be
found in isolation or combination.
Epidemiology
The exact incidence of posttraumatic stiffness is unknown.
In comparative studies on posttraumatic, postoperative, and primary shoulder stiffness being
managed during the same time period, the frequency of posttraumatic stiffness ranges from
12% to 23%.5,6
The incidence of posttraumatic shoulder stiffness is difficult to determine because many
patients may or may not associate a minor traumatic event to the onset of symptoms.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Alteration in scapular kinematics
Lack of capsular extensibility
Change in motor firing pattern of periscapular muscles with adaptive postural deviations
Pathomechanics of capsular ligamentous complex
Anterosuperior capsule (rotator interval) and upper subscapularis muscle: lead to loss of
external rotation in adduction
Inferior capsule: leads to considerable losses of abduction, forward flexion, and external and
internal rotation.? Posterosuperior capsule: rarely involved but causes loss of internal
rotation in adduction and in abduction

Anatomy and Biomechanics

Reeves7 demonstrated reduced capsular extensibility in posttraumatic stiff shoulders
with injected volumes of 5 to 9 cc; however, this was more than that injected in
idiopathic frozen shoulders (0.5 to 3 cc).
Elhassan et al6 compared a normal capsule, which is a few millimeters thick, with
capsules in patients with stiffness, which were 4 to 8 mm thick. In addition,
posttraumatic patients were most likely to have a thickened inferior capsule resulting in
limited flexion, abduction, and external and internal rotation.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Extra-articular: adhesions (eg, hematoma)
Neurologic: disruption of motor unit innervation (eg, brachial plexopathy)
Capsular: fibrosis (eg, sequelae of rotator cuff/capsular injury)
Intra-articular: injuries or scarring (eg, fracture)

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The stiffness that develops after soft-tissue or bony injury caused by an apparent
combination of capsular contracture and extracapsular adhesions.8 Most posttraumatic
stiffness is associated with a period of immobilization.1
Fracture of the proximal humerus leading to posttraumatic stiffness is most commonly
reported, but glenoid and clavicle fractures have been shown to lead to loss of motion.9
Neer10 reported that three- and four-part fractures managed nonsurgically or surgically
resulted in heterotopic ossification 12% of the time. Multiple attempts at closed
reduction, delayed surgical management of proximal humerus fractures, and associated
closed head injury all have been associated with a higher incidence of heterotopic
ossification. Bridging heterotopic ossification is unusual in the shoulder; however, it is an
indication for resection.11 Fifty percent of proximal humerus nonunions demonstrated
arthrofibrosis requiring lysis of the joint contracture at the time of open reduction and
internal fixation.12

Soft-tissue injury has been reported to lead to posttraumatic stiffness. Stiffness is
considerably more likely in patients diagnosed with a rotator cuff tear associated with a
traumatic event than in patients without trauma. In addition, full-thickness tears were
more likely to be associated stiffness than partial-thickness tears.3 Within animal rotator
cuff tear models, stiffness had a greater association with a neurologic injury than those
with a tendon injury alone.13
Evaluation/Diagnosis
(Figure 1)14
Figure 1 Algorithm for the evaluation of a patient with a history of trauma. (Adapted with
permission from Armstrong A: Diagnosis and clinical assessment of a stiff shoulder. Shoulder
Elbow 2015;7[2]:128-134.)
Patient History and Physical Examination
Clinical history

Thorough assessment of timing of the injury, progression of stiffness, associated pain,
timing, location, and changes in the character of the pain
Physical examination
Physical examination should include active and passive assessment of forward flexion and
abduction, internal and external rotation in adduction and abduction.
Reduction in the range of motion (ROM) and similar loss of active and passive motion
(compared with the contralateral side)

Patient History and Physical Examination
The patient history and physical examination are imperative for establishing the
diagnosis of posttraumatic stiffness. Occasionally, soft-tissue injuries leading to stiffness
are subtle and not able to be associated with subsequent decline in function. Conversely,
a patient may recall a nontraumatic event associated with shoulder pain and lack of
mobility.
Medical history, including diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, myocardial
infarction, malignancy with or without radiation therapy history, Dupuytren contracture,
complex regional pain syndrome, and neurologic or vascular disease, may predispose
patients to primary or other causes of shoulder stiffness and suggest an etiology other
than isolated posttraumatic shoulder stiffness. All shoulder surgery can result in
stiffness.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs are necessary to identify fractures, malunions, nonunions, and heterotopic bone.
Radiography is the first-line imaging modality to rule out other secondary causes of stiffness,
including tumors and arthritis.
Inclusion of an axillary radiograph is important to rule out missed dislocation.


Radiography
In patients with posttraumatic shoulder stiffness and normal radiographs, soft-tissue
injuries, including contusion and rotator cuff tendon tears should be considered.
Successful surgical management depends on an understanding of the specific anatomic
structures involved so appropriate repair and soft-tissue releases can be performed.2
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is performed in patients with posttraumatic stiffness resistant to nonsurgical
management if soft-tissue injury is suspected as the casual event.
MRI may show tendon injury, loose bodies, chondral lesions, or labral tearing not observed on
radiographs.
Magnetic resonance arthrography should be performed if the physical examination suggests
labral pathology.
Posttraumatic stiff shoulders may have associated capsular thickening.
MRI may not identify all posttraumatic causal lesions because some soft-tissue injuries will not
be detectable, even via advanced imaging studies, because of interval resolution.
Computed Tomography
CT can be performed in patients with posttraumatic stiffness to characterize fracture
nonunion or malunion, heterotopic ossification, and glenoid and proximal humerus
morphology (glenohumeral degenerative joint disease).
Management
Management should be targeted toward the underlying cause of posttraumatic stiffness.
Limited evidence is available on the management of posttraumatic shoulder stiffness.

Some studies have proposed nonsurgical treatment until a patient no longer has pain
associated with stiffness,2,15 whereas other studies have shown the results of surgical
treatment in patients with pain that persists and patients in whom a defined course of
nonsurgical treatment fails.6
Nonsurgical Management
NSAIDs
Steroid injections
Physical therapy

Nonsurgical Management
Posttraumatic stiffness may be minimized in patients with a nondisplaced proximal
humerus fracture via supervised physical therapy initiated within 14 days postinjury.16
Early management, whether nonsurgical or surgical, is suggested to limit long-term
stiffness and other associated sequelae in patients with a displaced proximal humerus
fracture.11 Very limited evidence exists because studies have isolated the outcomes of
the nonsurgical management of posttraumatic shoulder stiffness after it has manifested.
Nonsurgical management is empiric or based on the primary shoulder stiffness
literature.4,17,18
Surgical Management
Joint distention: no evidence to support effectiveness in patients with posttraumatic shoulder
stiffness
Manipulation: similar results to primary shoulder stiffness
Arthroscopic release: effective to reduce pain and improve motion; varying results compared
with primary and postoperative stiffness
Open reduction and internal fixation: suggested for surgical neck nonunion
Arthroplasty: radiostereometric analysis suggested for severe extra-articular tuberosity
malunions/nonunions or glenohumeral degenerative joint disease


Surgical Management
Reeves7 reported that, dissimilar from patients with primary shoulder stiffness, during
saline injection dilations, patients with posttraumatic shoulder stiffness did not sustain a
capsular rupture at the time of manipulation. In this case series, posttraumatic shoulder
stiffness improved with manipulation but not with serial dilation.7 No substantial
differences in ROM improvement were observed between patients with posttraumatic or
primary shoulder stiffness who underwent manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) at
early follow-up.5
Arthroscopic release has been shown to lead to improved ROM and pain in patients with
posttraumatic stiffness refractory to nonsurgical management.6,8,9,15,19,20 In comparing
posttraumatic and primary shoulder stiffness, the literature has shown mixed results for
functional outcomes after arthroscopic release. Gerber et al.19 reported poorer results
with posttraumatic shoulder stiffness compared with primary shoulder stiffness.
Holloway et al,20 Elhassan et al,6 and Nicholson8 reported equivalent outcomes. Three of
these studies reported improvement in comparing posttraumatic and postoperative
stiffness,6,19,20 whereas a smaller and further subdivided case series reported no
difference.8 Most of the discrepancies in the findings likely can be accounted for by the
heterogeneity of the etiology of posttraumatic (fracture/dislocation versus soft-tissue
injury) and postoperative (arthroscopic versus open) stiffness.
Several types of posttraumatic shoulder stiffness are not amenable to arthroscopic
release or MUA alone because of the underlying fracture malunion or nonunion. For
proximal humerus nonunions causing posttraumatic stiffness (Boileau type 3), studies
have supported open reduction and internal fixation.12,21,22 At the time of surgery,
arthrolysis can preformed to improve ROM and aid in fracture reduction. In patients with
a large, extra-articular tuberosity malunion (Bolieau type 4) or rotator cuff pathology
associated with muscle atrophy, reverse total shoulder arthroplasty should be
considered for management of the stiffness and underlying causal pathoanatomy22
(Figure 2).

Interscalene blocks and indwelling catheters with monitored anesthesia care for perioperative
pain management are useful to initiate early postoperative therapy.

Intraoperative Management
Manipulation should be performed cautiously because an isolated procedure for
posttraumatic stiffness is associated with a secondary risk of humeral fracture1 (Video 1)
Several studies have described their technique for arthroscopic capsule release.6,23,24
Arthroscopic capsulotomy includes:
Release of the rotator interval tissue to the coracoacromial ligament
Anterior capsule release at the base of the glenoid with preservation of the subscapularis
tendon
Direct release of the inferior capsule
Release of the posterior capsule to improve restricted internal rotation.1
Subacromial and subdeltoid lysis of adhesions should be performed before manipulation.
Open capsule release
Open release is infrequently performed secondary to advances in arthroscopy.
Open release may be indicated in patients in whom hardware may be removed and/or in
patients with severe posttraumatic stiffness and nonunion or malunion requiring
management via open reduction and internal fixation or reverse shoulder arthroplasty.
Video 1 Boston Medical Center: Surgical Technique for Adhesive Capsulitis: Arthroscopic Capsular
Technique [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020.

Postoperative Management
Early functional rehabilitation has been suggested.
Complications
Persistent stiffness: 1 of 21 (5%) in a case series9
Nerve injury: axillary nerve at risk with inferior capsule release
Fracture
Proximal humerus fracture has been reported with MUA and arthroscopic capsule release.7,9
Aggressive manipulation to restore rotation is not suggested.
Instability
Osteonecrosis
Pain
Infection
Effusion
Hematoma
Deep vein thrombosis/venous thromboembolism
Outcomes

Outcomes
MUA has been shown to result in no difference in ROM improvement in comparing
posttraumatic and idiopathic shoulder stiffness.5
Levy et al9 reported substantial improvement in posttraumatic shoulder stiffness in the
immediate postoperative period after arthroscopic capsule release. Nearly one-half of
the gains achieved surgically were lost by a follow-up of 6 months after completion of
supervised physical therapy. At final follow-up (mean, 33 months), patients had
improvement in motion beyond initial surgical improvement.
Most comparison studies report equivalent outcomes in comparing posttraumatic and
primary shoulder stiffness and slightly better results in comparing posttraumatic and

release.6,8,19,20
Postoperative Shoulder Stiffness
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Background
Patients with postoperative shoulder stiffness report dissatisfaction with pain management
and loss of shoulder motion in all planes.
The exact etiology of postoperative shoulder stiffness is unknown.
Fibrotic inflammation of the capsule (global or limited)
Scarring and adhesions between deltoid and the rotator cuff or the proximal humerus

Background
Postoperative, or secondary, shoulder stiffness is a dreaded, well-established
complication of open and arthroscopic shoulder surgery. It also is a pathologic process
characterized by biochemical and histopathologic changes and clinically debilitating
limitations of function. It has long been described as “difficult to define, difficult to treat,
and difficult to explain.”18 Patients with postoperative shoulder stiffness report
dissatisfaction with pain management and loss of shoulder motion in all planes.25
Epidemiology
Prevalence of 5% to 33% after shoulder surgery and more common after open shoulder
surgery compared with arthroscopic surgery
Initially successful postoperative rehabilitation with progressive worsening, increasing pain,
and gradual loss of active and passive motion
Most resolves within 6 months


Epidemiology
The incidence of adhesive capsulitis in the general population is approximately 3% to 5%
but as high as 20% within the diabetic population. It may arise idiopathically or
secondary to trauma or surgery.26 (Resource 1). The reported prevalence after shoulder
surgery is 5% to 33%, and it is more common after open shoulder surgery compared
with arthroscopic surgery. Posttraumatic adhesive capsulitis often is regarded as a self-
limiting disease that resolves between 6 months and 3 years; however, various studies
have shown that long-lasting symptoms may develop in 20% to 50% of patients.27
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Exact etiology unknown
Most likely related to surgical violation of tissue planes (rotator interval), causing contracture
of capsule
Capsular contractures and postoperative adhesions in surrounding soft tissues likely are
considered.
Histology
Stage I: inflammatory cell infiltration of synovium
Stage II: synovial proliferation
Stage III: dense collagenous tissue within the capsule

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Many theories exist with regard to the etiology of stiffness; however, the exact
pathophysiology remains unknown.26 Current understanding of the pathogenesis
involves an inflammatory phase followed by scar deposition and subsequent capsular
contracture. These phases typically correlate clinically with a pain-dominant presentation
followed by a stiffness phase. The phases also correlate with histologic findings of a
synovial inflammatory cell infiltrate followed by synovial proliferation and dense
collagenous tissue deposition in the capsule.26 The inflammatory stage or cascade
typically is characterized by transforming growth factor-beta– and tumor necrosis factor-

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001167
14/28

alpha–mediated recruitment of B and T lymphocytes and macrophages.26 A study on the
histology of excised coracohumeral ligament tissue found a proliferation of fibroblasts
with transformation of some to myofibroblasts, which is a process similar to that
observed in patients with Dupuytren contracture.27 This transformation to smooth
muscle myofibroblasts is thought to substantially contribute to the late stages of
capsular contracture and eventual fibrosis.
Risk Factors
Various risk factors are associated with postoperative shoulder stiffness, including diabetes
mellitus, hypothyroidism, infection, prior keloid formation, calcific tendinitis, history of
complex regional pain syndrome or gastroesophageal disorders, workers’ compensation, age
younger than 50 years, and female sex.

Risk Factors
Numerous risk factors have been identified in the development of postoperative
shoulder stiffness, including female sex, age older 40 years, history of trauma, human
leukocyte antigen-B27 positivity, and prolonged shoulder immobilization.25 A recent
meta-analysis suggested a genetic predisposition to adhesive capsulitis , noting a higher
incidence of this condition in White patients, patients with a positive family history, and
patients with human leukocyte antigen-B27 positivity.27 Endocrine abnormalities,
particularly diabetes mellitus), have been implicated in primary and secondary adhesive
capsulitis and may be the strongest associated risk factor. Interestingly, patients with
type 1 or type 2 diabetes have an increased risk for adhesive capsulitis , with a
prevalence of 10.3% and 22.4% respectively (Resource 1).28 Thyroid disorders, clinical
and subclinical hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, also appear to be another
substantial risk factor for idiopathic and postoperative shoulder stiffness.29 These risk
factors and comorbidities are important to note because they confer a poorer overall
long-term functional prognosis.

9/3/26, 5:49 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001167
15/28

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
A detailed patient history is important to help determine the etiology of postoperative stiffness
(poor pain control, prolonged immobilization, poorly controlled risk factors, diabetes mellitus,
infection, etc.).
The initial evaluation of patients with postoperative shoulder stiffness requires a thorough
physical examination, including skin sensitivity (nerve involvement), muscle defects (nerve
involvement), signs of infection (Cutibacterium acnes), and referred pain (cervical spine).
Physical examination of the shoulder reveals limited active ROM that is equal to passive range
of motion.
A complete shoulder examination should be performed to evaluate for any concomitant
shoulder disease (acromioclavicular joint, biceps, instability, rotator cuff re-tear).
Rotator cuff repair
Stiffness typically is global, and patients may report pain and weakness.
May have initial period of normal postoperative rehabilitation with progressive loss of
motion
Shoulder instability
Typically, loss of external rotation or other ROM
Open repair is associated with a higher risk for postoperative shoulder stiffness.
Arthroplasty
Most commonly related to posttraumatic stiffness after arthroplasty
Must evaluate for postoperative infection (C acnes)

Patient History and Physical Examination
Surgeons must elicit a thorough patient history to identify causes and risk factors that
help guide management and prognosis. In the postoperative setting, surgeons must
initially rule out infection, especially with C acnes, after the early postoperative period.
Full- and partial-thickness rotator cuff tears, glenohumeral and acromioclavicular
arthritis, calcific tendinitis, cervical radiculopathy, hardware irritation from
malpositioning, and fracture also may lead to substantial shoulder stiffness and must be
differentiated. An important feature of postoperative adhesive capsulitis is a similar loss
of active and passive motion.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001167
16/28

Most patients typically exhibit marked loss of active and passive shoulder motion,
especially with the shoulder in 90° of abduction. Often, a loss of external rotation of 50%
or more is present, and in patients with the most severe stiffness, complete loss of
glenohumeral motion is observed. Manual stretching of the shoulder capsule at the
extremes of motion reveals a firm end point, which reproduces pain. Similarly, capsular
contracture results in a global limitation of translation of the shoulder. These findings
should not be confused with painful weakness resulting from other conditions, such as
rotator cuff disease. Full strength generally is maintained in patients with postoperative
adhesive capsulitis. Nonspecific provocative testing, such as impingement maneuvers,
also may elicit pain, confusing the underlying diagnosis. Subtle distinctions during the
physical examination may prove valuable but may be challenging to discern, even for
experienced clinicians.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs should be obtained to rule out other causes and assess implant placement,
evaluate for humeral migration, and assess glenohumeral joint articulation.
Ultrasonography and MRI often are of limited use but may be useful to evaluate for rotator
cuff re-tear or capsular hypertrophy.

Imaging Studies
A thorough clinical evaluation includes standard plain radiographs (true AP [Grashey]
view, outlet/scapular Y view, and axillary lateral view) to exclude other primary causes of
shoulder pain and stiffness, such as glenohumeral arthritis, acromioclavicular arthritis,
and calcific tendinitis. Advanced imaging studies typically are not necessary or warranted
in the primary evaluation of a patient with idiopathic frozen shoulder. Regardless, MRI
and magnetic resonance arthrography findings consistent with frozen shoulder are
noted. This includes thickening of the coracohumeral ligament, thickening and increased
signal in the capsule in the axillary recess, decreased overall capsular volume, and
subcoracoid fat obliteration in the rotator cuff interval. Specifically, the thickness of the
coracohumeral ligament also has been shown to correlate with clinical loss of internal
and external rotation.30 In addition, MRI also can be performed to exclude a rotator cuff
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:49 PM
AAOS | Posttraumatic and Postoperative Shoulder Stiffness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001167
17/28

re-tear as the etiology of limited ROM. Overuse of advanced imaging studies should be
avoided because the diagnosis usually can be reliably determined based on the patient
history, physical examination findings, and plain radiographs and is less useful if an
shoulder arthroplasty implant is present. Unnecessary advanced imaging studies may
have potentially deleterious clinical ramifications. A notable study reported a high false-
positive rate of rotator cuff tears, especially partial-thickness tears, or re-tears based on
preoperative MRI performed in patients who underwent arthroscopic capsule release for
frozen shoulder. This illustrates the important principle of focusing on clinical judgment
rather than advanced imaging studies, particularly in patients with a frozen shoulder.
Management
Initial management of postoperative shoulder stiffness is nonsurgical.
Surgical treatment is indicated in patients nonresponsive to nonsurgical treatment.
Nonsurgical Management
First-line treatment should include physical therapy, oral or intra-articular steroid injections,
and oral NSAIDs.
A modified rehabilitation protocol in at-risk patients has been shown to reduce the incidence
of postoperative shoulder stiffness.
Extracorporeal shock wave therapy has shown some benefit in a few studies.
Calcitonin is used as adjuvant therapy for pain control.
Limited results with hyaluronic acid and hydrodilation

Nonsurgical Management
The first step in selecting the best treatment option for postoperative adhesive capsulitis
is to identify the cause of the shoulder stiffness. Management of postoperative stiffness
follows the criteria used for all clinical conditions that lead to loss of ROM. Nonsurgical
and surgical treatment options are available to manage a stiff shoulder.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:49 PM
AAOS | Posttraumatic and Postoperative Shoulder Stiffness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001167
18/28

First-line treatment is nonsurgical, and surgery should be considered only after failure of
multiple nonsurgical treatment options. Physical therapy programs associated with
aggressive passive stretching and dynamic bracing are critical to any surgical or
nonsurgical treatment plan.
Oral anti-inflammatories, either NSAIDs or a short course of oral corticosteroids, may be
particularly helpful in reducing pain enough to make physical therapy tolerable.
Medications will not relieve pain immediately but are used to allow patients to effectively
participate in physical therapy. Narcotic agents do not have a role in the nonsurgical
management of frozen shoulder.
Corticosteroid injections decrease pain effectively in patients with early stages of
adhesive capsulitis. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized controlled trial, a
notable decrease in shoulder pain was noted at 6 weeks;31 however, the benefit
becomes unclear with longer-term follow-up. Regardless, intra-articular steroid
injections do seem to have a role in the treatment of patients with adhesive capsulitis.
Other nonsurgical treatment modalities also are important to note because surgical
management should be reserved for recalcitrant shoulder stiffness. Extracorporeal
shock wave therapy appears to afford notable improvement in the first 4 to 6 weeks and
is a low-risk alternative to corticosteroid injections for patients with diabetes mellitus
who may see an effect on their blood glucose control.32 Calcitonin therapy has been
identified as a potential effective augment for pain control in patients with adhesive
capsulitis. The current intranasal dose recommendation is 200 U (one puff) daily.33
Ultrasonography-guided hydrodistension has been reported to be effective in patients
with postoperative adhesive capsulitis in the short term; however, questions remain with
regard to the long-term benefits. Finally, hyaluronic acid injections in combination with
corticosteroid injections and physical therapy have been shown to result in excellent
outcomes, with complete resolution of adhesive capsulitis.34
Surgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:49 PM
AAOS | Posttraumatic and Postoperative Shoulder Stiffness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001167
19/28

Surgical treatment is reserved for patients who do not respond to nonsurgical treatment
within 6 months.
Manipulation Under Anesthesia
Can be performed under general anesthesia or a regional block
Randomized controlled trials showed no difference between MUA and arthroscopic capsule
release.
May not be as helpful after rotator cuff repair because of extra-articular adhesions
Technique
Gentle passive ROM is the goal.
Begin with forward flexion followed by external rotation with the arm at the side. This is
followed by cross-body adduction to release the posteroinferior capsule. Finally, the arm is
brought into abduction, and the arm is rotated into maximal external rotation followed by
internal rotation.
It is critical to maintain a short lever arm, control the arm proximally, and avoid holding the
forearm or wrist.

Technique
If nonsurgical management, including NSAIDs, physical therapy, and injections, fail to
provide symptom relief after 9 to 12 months, surgical management is indicated.
Currently, MUA and arthroscopic capsule release are two commonly used treatment
options. Arthroscopic synovectomy and circumferential capsulotomy have been shown
to result in long-lasting improvement in ROM and pain relief; however, many studies
have shown that MUA and capsular release to be equivalent in the relief of clinical
symptoms. In a systematic review of 22 studies that compared the outcomes of patients
treated via MUA and/or capsular release, Grant et al35 concluded that capsular release
may confer limited benefit instead of, or in addition to, MUA. Alternatively, many studies
have shown notable long-term effectiveness with arthroscopic capsule release.

Manipulative therapy should be performed in a gentle manner that avoids fracture or
ligament damage. Surgeons should focus on forward flexion first (elevation of the arm in
the sagittal plane while the scapula is stabilized by placing one hand along its axillary
border). The arm is then passively flexed forward in the sagittal plane to the maximum
possible extent. Passive external rotation is performed at 0° of abduction, followed by
external rotation at 90° of abduction, and finally internal rotation. Stabilization of the
scapula through each movement and maintenance of a short lever arm by controlling
the arm proximally and avoiding stress to the elbow joint, forearm, or wrist are critical.36
Arthroscopic Capsule Release
Indicated for shoulder stiffness secondary to capsular contraction and adhesions
Allows for evaluation of other intra-articular/subacromial causes of postoperative shoulder
stiffness
Technique
Release of the rotator interval, anterosuperior capsule, and posterosuperior capsule is
important (Video 1).

Technique
If a stiff shoulder is refractory to manipulative therapy, aggressive manipulation of the
scapulohumeral articulation may be dangerous. Arthroscopic capsule release is the
preferred technique for the management of postoperative shoulder stiffness caused by
capsule contraction and adhesion formation. It allows for precise and selective
débridement of scarred tissues and division of the shortened and thickened capsule via
partial capsulectomy. The target of the arthroscopic procedure is to release the
posterosuperior and anterosuperior capsule and the rotator interval.37 Finally, surgeons
must address the subacromial and subdeltoid spaces arthroscopically from anterior to
posterior, the lateral recess, and the bursal side of the rotator cuff extending medially to
the acromioclavicular joint and the scapular spine. Adhesions that limit motion may be

Postoperative Rehabilitation
Physical therapy should be initiated as soon as possible in the postoperative setting, as
early as postoperative day one. Regional anesthesia with the use of an interscalene block
or an indwelling catheter may provide adequate analgesia to allow for immediate
postoperative ROM. Mariano et al38 showed that a continuous interscalene block results
in greater pain relief, reduced opioid consumption, improved sleep quality, and overall
increased patient satisfaction; however, interscalene blocks are associated with some
risks. Reversible and phrenic nerve paralysis have been reported.39
The physical therapy protocol focuses on achieving or maintaining functional ROM via
slow sustained stretching. Patients are encouraged to perform daily stretching exercises,
including wall-walking for forward elevation, the doorway stretch for external rotation,
and the modified sleeper stretch for internal rotation. Patients often find stretching in
the shower to be more successful because of the heat. A sling is only used for a few days
postoperatively and must be discontinued by 1 week postoperatively. Patients are
encouraged not to sleep in the sling. Sleeping on an incline often is more comfortable
during the first postoperative week. Patients should be released from follow-up care

Complications
Complications related to surgical management include humeral shaft fracture, neurapraxia
(especially axillary nerve), rotator cuff injury, glenoid and labral injuries, and complex regional
pain syndrome.

Complications
Multiple complications have been reported in the management of postoperative
adhesive capsulitis. Complications of MUA include fractures, glenoid/labral injuries,
neuropraxia, and rotator cuff pathology. In a prospective trial, arthroscopic assessment
after MUA revealed multiple potential iatrogenic complications, including superior labral
tears, partial subscapularis tears, anterior labral detachments, and tears of the middle
glenohumeral ligament.40
Arthroscopic capsule release, while resulting in improved outcomes in patients with
adhesive capsulitis, is associated with its own unique set of complications, including
axillary nerve injury and, rarely, complex regional pain syndrome.41
Outcomes
Nonsurgical management resolves symptoms in 90% of patients.
Patients usually regain ROM similar to that of the contralateral side if arthroscopic capsule
release is performed.

Stiffness can be prevented via early motion or via a period of immobilization. Adhesive
capsulitis, even in the postoperative period, is considered to be self-resolving; however,
the debilitating nature of functional limitations often drives patients to undergo
nonsurgical or surgical treatment for the disease. Nonsurgical treatment options, such
as injections and long-term physical therapy, appear to resolve symptoms in as many as
90% of patents.34 Le Lievre and Murrell42 reported patients regained ROM similar to that
of the contralateral shoulder 7 years after arthroscopic capsule release.
Postoperative shoulder stiffness must be considered because it is a complication of
shoulder surgery that substantially affects quality of life and patient satisfaction. Being
aware of risk factors that may predispose patients to frozen shoulder is important for
patient counseling and shared decision making.
